correctness.rationale: The Katz resolvent yields exact triangle, path, and pendant-graph centrality expressions B, L, P. All unilateral deviation types from cyclic triangle sponsorship are compared, with the isolate's maximum per-edge addition payoff established by symmetry and supermodularity of walk indicators. Explicit positive rational differences establish ell<U<V for 0<q<1/3, hence a strict open region and the exact weak support threshold. Every possible triangle sponsorship orientation has a sponsor paying at most U and the isolate must pay at least V, proving the sharp minimum global cost ratio. The only three-vertex non-core–periphery graph, an edge plus isolate, fails Nash because C3-2B2=2q^3/((1-q)(1-2q^2))>0. The exact-rational checker independently recomputes utilities and all unilateral deviations at seven rational q values, yielding 392 comparisons; exhaustive finite checks do not substitute for the symbolic proof.

originality.rationale: The closest full primary work proves core–periphery shape under homogeneous linear costs; its Example 1 already realizes K3 plus isolate with a distinct nonlinear benefit. The present claim instead identifies necessary-and-sufficient Katz support inequalities under player-specific costs, attains the globally least dispersion for that graph, shows the ratio tends to unity, and excludes smaller non-core equilibria. Related literature uses directed weighted budget-constrained Katz choice, shortest-path benefits, or bilateral pairwise stability, none entailing the exact unilateral Katz theorem. Available index and text searches found no same implication; this is best-knowledge originality, not absolute priority certification.

value.rationale: The homogeneous-cost structural theorem suggests a natural robustness question: does a positive uniform heterogeneity margin preserve core–periphery for the same Katz centrality? The counterexample proves no, quantitatively: exactly R(q)>1 is required for the simplest non-core network, with R(q)->1. Exact necessary-and-sufficient support inequalities reveal a nonempty strict Nash region, while a separate three-agent impossibility proves a sharp structural size boundary. The result is neither merely a borrowed graph shape nor an arbitrary finite computation; it gives a meaningful structural boundary for an emerging network game. It does not claim a full architecture classification or fixed-q vanishing heterogeneity.
